title: AI in Drug R&D: At Last, the End of the Beginning - TimmermanReport.com
gist: Synthesizing a Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Perspective led by Andreas Bender and an essay by insitro's Daphne Koller, the piece argues AI in biopharma has delivered impressive technical performance without clinically relevant productivity gains because effort concentrates where labeled data and fast scorecards already exist — hit and ligand discovery — rather than where leverage is greatest, Phase II clinical success. The constraint is predictive validity and missing human biology, not model sophistication, and the economics of building better proxies favor foundations and precompetitive consortia over single companies.

themes.theme: When AI actually works: the information environment

insights.claim: AI performs especially well when three conditions align: enough observations that genuinely bear on the question, an objective specified well enough to optimize against, and feedback that is fast, cheap and trustworthy enough to learn from.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A three-part screen for judging whether any AI-biotech claim sits in a tractable domain or is being sold into a hostile information environment.
insights.locator: What kind of problems is AI good at?

insights.claim: AlphaFold succeeded in an unusually favorable information environment — decades of experimental ground truth plus protein folding conserved enough to pool information across enormous evolutionary distances — so invoking it as proof of what AI will do next in drug discovery is a category error.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Direct rebuttal to the most common bull argument in AI-biotech fundraising decks; discount pitches whose core proof point is AlphaFold.
insights.quote: AlphaFold was a magnificent achievement, but it was also an achievement in a domain whose informational structure was unusually well suited to AI.
insights.locator: Protein structure prediction offered an unusually favorable

insights.claim: Stephen Wolfram's 'pockets of reducibility' — bounded problems where available information and feedback are good enough for computational traction — maps AI's real opportunity space in R&D: protein structure is one pocket, portions of molecular design and some operational aspects of clinical development are others.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Gives a map for where AI-pharma revenue is actually addressable today versus where it is aspirational — useful for sizing vendor TAM claims.
insights.locator: Can we create new pockets?

insights.claim: Channeling Robert Solow, the Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Perspective asks why AI is visible everywhere in biopharma except in the productivity statistics, concluding that evidence of clinically relevant impact is disappointingly limited.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The productivity-statistics test is the cleanest falsifier for AI-pharma narratives; until it moves, the sector's re-rating rests on promise, not output.
insights.locator: Our argument: start with what matters

insights.claim: Drug R&D has absorbed recombinant proteins, genomics and high-throughput technologies in succession without an obvious corresponding improvement in aggregate R&D productivity, so per Jack Scannell, AI bending that trajectory would accomplish what other extraordinarily important innovations did not.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Sets the historical base rate: prior platform revolutions in biotech did not lift aggregate productivity, so the burden of proof on AI is unusually high.
insights.quote: That sets a considerably higher bar for “transformation” than demonstrating impressive technical performance.
insights.locator: There is also a sobering historical backdrop

insights.claim: Modeling equivalent improvements in speed, cost or probability of success across drug development shows that improving clinical success, especially around Phase II, has the greatest leverage, yet most AI work remains concentrated far earlier in hit and ligand discovery where labeled data are plentiful.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The value-per-unit-improvement is concentrated at Phase II; AI vendors serving discovery are addressing the low-leverage segment of the value chain.
insights.quote: But it risks becoming the familiar search for the keys under the streetlight, focusing on what we can readily model rather than what most needs improving.
insights.locator: One place we start is by asking where an improvement

insights.claim: Computational effort in drug R&D naturally gravitates toward places where data and scorecards already exist, giving some efforts a self-satisfying quality of pursuing what is available rather than what is actually most useful.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Explains persistent misallocation in AI-pharma spending — a structural reason the sector's capex has not translated into approvals.
insights.quote: It also gives some of these efforts a certain self-satisfying, almost onanistic quality, pursuing what is available rather than what is actually most useful.
insights.locator: This makes the uneven progress of AI considerably less mysterious

insights.claim: Biology's 'epistemic opacity' means the relationship between the proxy that can readily be measured and the clinical outcome actually cared about is often poorly understood, so both measurements and models sit far from what matters to drug developers and patients.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Names the core reason model accuracy fails to convert to clinical success — a diligence question that cuts through AI-platform performance metrics.
insights.locator: Much of the problem is that both the things we’re measuring

insights.claim: Biological data are highly conditional: results in one cell type at one concentration in one experimental system may say little about a particular patient, and ostensibly identical experiments can give materially different answers in another laboratory, which makes pooling datasets across assays and conditions deceptive rather than additive.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Undermines the 'we aggregated the largest biological dataset' moat claim — scale assembled across heterogeneous conditions may encode noise, not signal.
insights.locator: Biological data are also highly conditional

insights.claim: The binding constraint in biomedical AI is predictive validity — whether the measurable thing tells us something useful about the outcome we care about — not data quantity or technical quality, since exquisitely reproducible data around a weak proxy merely characterizes the wrong thing with greater precision.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The single most transferable diligence lens in the piece: ask what the proxy predicts and whether that link was established or assumed.
insights.quote: Generating exquisitely reproducible data around a weak proxy mostly allows us to characterize the wrong thing with greater precision.
insights.locator: This is why saying that biomedicine has enormous amounts of data

insights.claim: Databases such as ChEMBL and PubChem contain more than a million known bioactive ligands while marketed drugs number only in the thousands, so AI can become extraordinarily good at generating ligands without producing correspondingly more drugs.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A roughly 1000:1 ratio quantifying the ligand-to-drug attrition that generative chemistry does not address — the key number for valuing AI molecule-design platforms.
insights.locator: The numerical contrast is striking

insights.claim: Binding to a target is only one of many drug requirements, alongside workable physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties, sufficient selectivity, adequate tissue exposure, an acceptable safety profile and human efficacy, per Brown and Goldstein's Magritte-inspired observation that a gene sequence is not a drug.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A checklist for stress-testing AI-designed-molecule announcements: potency headlines say nothing about the five other gates a candidate must clear.
insights.locator: Brown & Goldstein (inspired by Magritte) observed

insights.claim: Two models with nearly identical standard overall performance can behave completely differently in use — one better at surfacing the few compounds worth advancing, the other better at rejecting compounds with liabilities — so there is no context-free definition of a good model, only what a model is good for.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Benchmark leaderboards are close to meaningless for procurement decisions in pharma AI; ask which decision the model improves instead.
insights.quote: There is no context-free definition of a good model; the relevant question is what the model is good for.
insights.locator: The same issue arises in how models themselves are evaluated

insights.claim: A model earns its keep only if it changes which experiment gets run, which compound advances, or which weak program gets killed; absent those links to project context and downstream decision-making, better model performance need not translate into better drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption test for pharma AI vendors — decision-change is the revenue-durable outcome, not model metrics.
insights.locator: A model operates inside an actual project

insights.claim: Tej Azad, Harlan Krumholz and Suchi Saria argue in parallel that clinical AI readiness is a property of a model-task-context pairing rather than of a model, compressed into the prescription 'study form = use form' — evaluate the tool with the users, information, constraints and consequences it will actually encounter.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Convergent evidence from clinical AI that deployment-context evaluation is becoming the standard — a likely direction for regulatory expectations on health AI.
insights.locator: make a strikingly parallel argument about clinical AI

insights.claim: The prescription is less technology push and more science pull: start with the decisions and clinical outcomes most in need of improvement, then work backward to the measurements and experimental systems that can inform them, since a gorgeous model may be only a prestige publication.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Distinguishes AI-biotech companies organized around decisions from those organized around models — a durable sorting criterion for the sector.
insights.quote: A gorgeous model may represent a succès d’estime and a prestige publication. What matters is whether it improves consequential R&D decisions.
insights.locator: Hence our call (familiar to TR readers)

themes.theme: Koller: keys for the wrong locks

insights.claim: Daphne Koller argues the 'magic wand' vision of AI-driven cures rests on the seductive assumption that we already understand human biology well enough for a clever AI to find cures hidden in what we know, and her answer is 'We don't' — aimed at barely-measured biology, AI may mostly help generate failures faster.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The most credible AI-native voice in biotech is publicly bearish on the near-term magic-wand thesis — a notable sentiment marker for AI-biotech valuations.
insights.quote: Aimed at biology we have only begun to measure and barely understand, she writes, AI may mostly help us generate failures faster.
insights.locator: Koller writes that she fully expects AI eventually

insights.claim: Scannell's parallel observation is that feeding AI with data from poor biological models simply increases the number of wrong answers you can generate per second.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Compute scaling on invalid models is negative-yield — argues against the 'more GPUs will solve biology' capital allocation thesis.
insights.quote: feeding AI with data from poor biological models simply increases the number of wrong answers you can generate per second
insights.locator: This conclusion mirrors Scannell’s recent observation

insights.claim: Koller divides drug discovery into disease-to-mechanism, mechanism-to-drug and drug-to-patient, and notes AI's most visible progress has come in the middle task — designing proteins, small molecules and other agents against a given mechanism — leaving the harder biological question largely untouched, so we are getting good at manufacturing keys that are often for the wrong locks.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: A three-stage map for segmenting AI-biotech companies; those clustered in mechanism-to-drug are competing in the least-differentiating stage.
insights.quote: We are getting pretty good at manufacturing keys, as she memorably puts it, but they are often keys for the wrong locks.
insights.locator: Koller divides drug discovery into three broad tasks

insights.claim: About a quarter of drug-target pairs in the 2024 pipeline were concentrated around only 37 targets, each with more than 50 drugs directed against it, even as the total pipeline nearly doubled over the preceding decade while the annual number of novel targets entering the pipeline fell sharply.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Quantifies extreme target crowding — a direct read on competitive intensity and pricing pressure in the classes everyone is chasing, and on the scarcity premium for genuinely novel mechanisms.
insights.locator: Koller sees one consequence in the remarkable crowding

insights.claim: Binding chemistry is much less often the limiting problem in drug development than it once was, while stronger evidence that a target genuinely drives disease substantially improves the odds of clinical success — though efficacy failure can also stem from inadequate target engagement, tissue exposure, or trial design and execution.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Target-validation evidence, not chemistry capability, is the variable that shifts probability of success — the thing to underwrite in a preclinical asset.
insights.locator: To be sure, clinical efficacy failure is not synonymous

insights.claim: Bytes and coverage do not move together in biology: hundreds of millions of single cells sound enormous but sample relatively few perturbations across relatively few cellular contexts, before even adding disease state, dose, time or combinations of perturbations.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Deflates single-cell atlas scale as a moat; perturbation and context coverage is the metric that matters for foundation-model-style biology bets.
insights.quote: bytes and coverage do not move together
insights.locator: There is also a deeper data problem

insights.claim: The biology that matters most is often the least transferable: protein folding generalizes across species unusually well while neurodegenerative disease does not, and the slowest-progress diseases sit toward the human-specific end where measurements are most expensive, least available and most ethically constrained.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Explains why AI gains will be highly uneven by therapeutic area — expect least benefit precisely in CNS/neurodegeneration where unmet need and failure rates are highest.
insights.locator: But (to borrow a phrase immortalized by Commentary’s Abe Greenwald)

insights.claim: Koller explicitly rejects the need to map all human biology first, writing 'We don't need a universal causal model in order to make medicines,' and instead advocates targeted models that make particular regions of biological space navigable toward a desired outcome.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The constructive path for AI-biotech: bounded, purpose-built biological models rather than universal foundation models of the cell.
insights.quote: We don’t need a universal causal model in order to make medicines,
insights.locator: There is a silver lining, of sorts

insights.claim: Mechanistic understanding is not the only route to prediction — a strong phenotypic model, human genetics, a validated biomarker, or an AI-discovered empirical pattern as described by Obermeyer and colleagues can all supply useful predictive information despite incomplete causal explanation, provided the observable is reliably connected to what eventually happens in people.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Widens the set of investable approaches beyond mechanism-first platforms — genetics-anchored and phenotype-first companies satisfy the same requirement.
insights.locator: Of course, while mechanistic understanding is a powerful route

insights.claim: AI improves rapidly only where feedback is fast, accurate and cheap — code has a compiler, molecular design has rapid quantitative assays — whereas drug development's ultimate scorecard requires a human clinical trial taking years, costing millions and constrained by the pace of living biology.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: The scorecard asymmetry is why software-style AI improvement curves cannot be extrapolated to pharma; it caps how fast any AI-native biotech can compound learning.
insights.quote: Code has a compiler, she notes.
insights.locator: Koller’s other especially useful contribution is the scorecard

insights.claim: No amount of compute can make a neurodegenerative disease progress faster to reveal sooner whether a drug worked, so the pace of clinical development remains limited by biology rather than computation even as AI improves patient identification, site selection, regulatory drafting and data management.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Bounds the realistic near-term AI opportunity in clinical development to operational efficiency — real, monetizable, but not timeline-transformative.
insights.locator: No amount of compute can make a neurodegenerative disease

insights.claim: Creating new pockets of computational traction requires deliberately generating fit-for-purpose data rather than applying AI to whatever happens to be available, with the critical step being to establish that an experimental proxy really predicts the in vivo or clinical outcome before generating data and models at scale.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Purpose-built data generation is the differentiating capex in AI-biotech; companies scraping existing public data are building on the weakest foundation.
insights.locator: Our paper argues for starting with consequential R&D decisions

insights.claim: Koller's prescription is to measure more relevant human biology — particularly how biological systems respond to perturbation — and use AI for targeted causal models, which could yield better clinical readouts that identify likely responders, confirm target engagement and detect disease-biology changes earlier, letting trials enroll better, read out sooner and catch failures earlier rather than merely running more efficiently.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Earlier failure detection is the largest available NPV lever in pharma R&D; watch perturbation-biology data generators as the enabling layer.
insights.locator: Koller places greater emphasis on improving our understanding

insights.claim: Biomarker validation is far harder than the concept suggests: the author's experience in Experimental Medicine at Merck nearly two decades ago showed the volume of validation work required before an organization would kill or redirect a program on a biomarker result was substantial, and persuading a regulator to accept a biomarker as a trial endpoint is a far higher bar still.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Tempers timelines for any thesis that AI-derived biomarkers will shorten trials — regulatory acceptance, not discovery, is the rate-limiting step.
insights.quote: A proxy is not a shortcut simply because it can be measured sooner.
insights.locator: But doing so is difficult, as I learned in my first industry role

insights.claim: Per Scannell, a company inventing a proprietary molecule can capture much of the value it creates, but a better translational model, assay or validated biomarker also benefits competitors, so validated proxies can be enormously valuable to patients while being hard for the funding organization to monetize.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Explains structural underinvestment in the highest-leverage R&D input and predicts that this layer gets funded by foundations, public funders and precompetitive consortia rather than by industry.
insights.locator: There is an economic challenge as well

insights.claim: Creating appropriately designed, harmonized biomedical datasets may require efforts beyond the capacity or incentives of any single organization, pointing to a role for disease foundations, public funders and carefully designed precompetitive consortia.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Consortium and foundation formation is the leading indicator to watch for whether the AI-in-pharma bottleneck actually gets addressed.
insights.locator: Our Perspective acknowledges that creating appropriately designed

insights.claim: Realizing a new technology's value generally requires more than substituting a new tool for an old one and over time changes how the work itself gets done, enabling different ways of organizing information, collaborating and making decisions — but AI must first help scientists make better consequential decisions.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Organizational redesign, not license count, determines whether pharma AI spend produces returns — a signal to look for in large-pharma AI disclosures.
insights.locator: There is also a distinct organizational dimension

insights.claim: The productive framing has shifted from whether 'AI' works globally to where the technology has the information, problem structure and feedback required to help now, and where better science can create those conditions — treating AI as an earthbound capability rather than a source of salvation or ruin.
insights.speaker: Timmerman Report
insights.so_what: Marks a sentiment inflection from abstraction to capability profiling — expect diligence, disclosure and pricing of AI-pharma deals to get more granular.
insights.locator: From abstraction to capability
